passages.text: The Mournful Book of Johannes of Trittenheim, abbot of Sponheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, of the Bursfeld Observance, on the condition and ruin of the monastic order, no less useful than pleasing to religious and devout men.
To the venerable and most beloved father, lord Blasius, abbot of the monastery of Hirsau: brother Johannes, called abbot in Sponheim, sends greeting and charity.

Although your request and that of your brothers, dearest father, far exceeds the powers of my talent, nevertheless I have preferred to undertake the arduous burden rather than fail, as far as I can, to satisfy your charity. For love of God, zeal for the order, and fervor for discipline make you worthy that I should deny you nothing when you ask for the honor of God. You asked me, when I was present, with words; when absent, with frequent letters; and in a certain way you compelled me by the authority of your presidency to write something to you about the calamity of our order, so that you might stir the fathers, to be assembled with you in chapter, to compassion for it.

The request is holy, but the difficulty of obedience is great. I know I shall be torn by the teeth of the envious, who will judge me presumptuous, and [unclear] the things that lie open to the eyes of all. If they do not wish these things to be written, let them grieve that they were even done. In this work only charm of speech is lacking; and for this I do not fear being blamed among religious men. By whom? Is truth therefore despised because it is not clothed in the ornament of eloquence? Far from it. Better is plain and true speech than ornate and false speech. But these matters are nothing to the point. I therefore submit this little work to your examination, so that, if you judge it worthy, it may be read to the brothers; but if unworthy, it may flee the eyes of the lords. Farewell. In the year of the Lord 1493, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May.
Here begins the mournful book of lord Johannes, abbot of Sponheim, on the ruin of the order of our holy father Benedict.

When I call back to mind the former beauty of our order, I grieve vehemently over the deformity which it now suffers, so that I would rather shed tears than compose a mournful discourse. For who would not weep over its ruin, if he weighs its ancient glory? O, if only we would at some time recall to memory the once golden ages of this most sacred order, when, like a river of paradise in doctrine and holiness, it watered the whole Church throughout the world, we would easily perceive that its present condition is nothing. Indeed our observance, which we call regular, when compared with the institutions of the ancients, is found not only lesser, but in many respects more lax. How the gold has grown dim; how the finest color has changed! The splendor of extraordinary holiness, once gleaming, has been darkened by desire for earthly things; the rule of honor has yielded to the enticements of pleasures. Therefore let my eyes bring forth tears by day and by night, and let them not be silent, because the religion of my people has been crushed with a great crushing, with a very grievous wound. If I go out to the fields, behold the idle and vain; if I enter the monasteries, behold those wasted by pleasures. For I find many professors of the rule of father Benedict; I discern few walking according to his tradition. “You have multiplied the nation,” says the prophet to the Lord, “you have not increased the joy,” because, since the holy exercises of monks fail in many, corrupt hearts do not admit the true joy that is born of virtue. If only we would awaken, even late at last, after the destruction of so many souls, which, despising the yoke of regular observance, have descended into the abyss of damnation. If only we feared the sentence of Benedict our lawgiver, who so often [unclear] God

[unclear]: he strikes at the madness of a harsh abbot. Now therefore my discourse must be directed to you, most reverend fathers: you who, by apostolic authority, celebrate the order; you who receive the power of compelling rebels to discipline; you who have zeal for our order according to knowledge. You, therefore, I address; to you I shall try, according to my powers, to persuade that you come to the aid of an order almost falling; and I most earnestly exhort you to do this.

Consider, fathers, the miserable condition of our religion, and, so far as you are able, come to the aid of its calamity, if indeed you wish to endure to the end. The wickedness of many is not hidden from you: in order that they may be able to escape the discipline of the order, they labor to dismember themselves from it. Their rashness must be firmly opposed, lest the unpunished malice of a few give many the boldness to offend. And the wickedness of a few, when deferred, always increases. Although the public good ought not to be corrupted by the evil of one person, nevertheless the ignorant crowd blames all for the fault of a few. Therefore, those evil men who by their own deformity cloud the reputation of the good are strengthened by superiors who do not punish them.

It therefore belongs to you, fathers, to correct deformed monks as far as possible; it is the duty of your office to preserve the order in its vigor. And because a fool is not corrected by speech, what our hierophant set down against the incorrigible, as it were monastically, should generally be referred to [unclear]. Rise up now, fathers, for it is time. Arm yourselves with zeal for regular discipline. I beg you, defend the inheritance of the blessed father Benedict. Drive out the proud; correct the rebellious; rebuke the hard. Fight bravely for the preservation of our order. Arm yourselves with the armor of God and with love of the order, about to fight not so much by your own labors as by the help of Christ. His grace will furnish you aid, if with purity of heart you pour out devout prayers to him.

Why then do you dissemble? Why do you not defend the portion of Saint Benedict? How long will the efforts of the wicked prevail against the holy order? Truly, fathers, truly, the great necessity of the order demands a swift remedy. Consider the conduct of irregular abbots and monks, and weigh how wickedly they kick against the discipline of the order. Apart from the habit, and that itself in many cases dissolute, they show nothing honorable or religious. But reserving these things for their appointed places, let us hasten to what we have intended.
On the Most Holy Primitive State of Our Order. Chapter 2.

I somewhat doubt whether I shall do a thing pleasing to all if I commend in a few words the former state of our order, since I judge that by the praises of the ancients I have paid little regard to the monks of our own time. For there are some who think themselves either the best monks, or dare to compare themselves with those best fathers who preceded us. However they measure themselves, let them not be angry with me if I do not dare to equate our observance with that of the ancients. For if we contemplate their life by a right light, we shall scarcely be able to compare the best among us, in habit, with a good monk of that time.

Indeed, their holy way of life, bright with virtues, approved by signs, and illustrious through instruction in all the Scriptures, won favor with God and with men. For hearing the voice of the Lord saying, “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me,” they flew to monasteries, despising the world; and, placing their necks under the yoke of the rule, they humbly took up the norm of obedience. Loving God with their whole heart, they sought nothing worldly in this life; but, all perishable things despised, and tested in the furnace of poverty, they happily arrived at the heavenly kingdom.

They were mature men, zealous, and most learned: firm in faith, strengthened in hope, shining with twofold charity; pure in mind, outstanding in devotion, and adorned with the honor of every virtue. They had no care for earthly things, no enticement of pleasures was in them; but, turned toward God with all their powers, they conquered the world with its vanities. Hence kings and princes of this age, devout men and dear to God, because of the most holy way of life of the monks, became lovers of the order, and magnificently exalted it with gifts and largesses.

[unclear]. They rejoiced that in their times the holy pursuits of monks were being enlarged and extended with glory even to the remotest regions of the world. For the holy monks, the more they loved God, the more they were also loved by men. And the less they sought earthly things, the more, by God’s providence, they abounded in what was necessary for the body. For to those who love God, the whole world is riches.

O how comely is the face of your youth, holy religion of Benedict; how fair your aspect, how adorned your majesty with the splendor of all virtues. Who could suffice to weigh you worthily? You offer the way of three days to the people of God, freed in the desert from the servitude of Pharaoh, when you persuade men, taken out of the darkness of the world, to come by the three substantial vows of religion to the desert of cenobitic life for the love of God. Blessed are the professors who, withdrawing from the Egypt of this world, pant with all their desires along this way of three days toward the land of the eternal promise.

This is the threefold cord of holy religion, which is not easily broken, which is adorned with the brightness of obedience, chastity, and poverty; which calls back its lovers to the heavenly homeland; which presents its cultivators joyful to the supreme emperor, Christ Jesus. For although many things are necessary for regular observance, yet I would dare to say that whoever has kept these three inviolate stands secure in the order, like a threefold cord. For all the statutes of the order were made for the preservation of these substantial things.

The holy monks of old, attentively considering this, observed this way of the three substantial things with the greatest zeal: poor in spirit through contempt of all worldly things; continent through chastity of mind and body; obedient through humble subjection; and rich in every virtue. They shone forth most renowned in learning and holiness, and by word as well as by example converted many from injustice. Hence, as their merits advanced, many of them were promoted to the governments of churches; and the higher they had been placed, the more renowned they became in virtues. What church would not seek a priest from the order of Benedict? What people devoted to the Christian name would not desire a teacher from the college of monks? For to many

[unclear] in the order of the holy father Benedict, men most excellent in every kind of learning and holiness, were illustrious, as almost all who wrote ancient histories testify. And indeed, to speak without envy, the holy religious order of Benedict easily surpasses all, if you wish to consider dignity, if its broad dominion throughout the world, if men distinguished for learning and holiness, if finally their multitude. For this venerable plant brought forth [unclear]; archprelates, one thousand six hundred; bishops, three thousand five hundred. But if anyone calls this total of illustrious prelates too great and casts doubt upon it, let him turn over the chronicles and deeds of the ancients, and he will find that few have been named out of many. But let no one think that the former splendor of the order should be measured by the present, since there is no equal comparison of our men with it, when in our times monks do not shine, as formerly, either in knowledge of the Scriptures or in holiness of morals. Perhaps even now you will find devout monks, though few, but simple. But for the rule of souls in this time devotion does not suffice, if knowledge of the Scriptures is lacking. But if our monks are neither devout nor learned, they are rightly judged unworthy for the rule of churches. Many subjects, indeed, walk well, who, if they have been raised to the governance of others, have never remained in the tranquillity of their former life. And, to say briefly what I think: neither are monks worthy of churches, nor churches of monks, at this time. The cause is not hidden from the prudent; it is to be brought into the light hereafter, in its own time. Now, if it please, let us inquire briefly what the present state of our order is.
On the Present Lamentable State of Our Order. Chapter iii.
My eyes have failed from weeping; my inward parts are truly troubled; my liver has been poured out upon the earth, over

[unclear] of my order: when the humble little one [unclear] in it; when, cast down and without honor, it lies open to the hands of the enemy. Let no one despise me as I mourn; let no one blame my grief. I do not seek earthly honors; I do not aspire to ecclesiastical dignities, but I groan that learning and holiness have fallen away from my order. What have we to do with empty honors, we who seek life in heaven? Alas, the crown of our head has fallen; monastic devotion has grown lukewarm; charity has grown cold; the honor of regular discipline has for the most part failed. Where now in our order, and in its most holy men, is the devotion once so abundant? Where, in every variety of writings, is venerable learning? Where is the solicitude of abbots for the care of the Lord’s flock? We see many monasteries founded according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, in which, apart from the name and the habit, we see no trace of regular discipline. Over this, O fathers, take up lamentation; deplore the ruin of our most holy order, if perhaps God may turn to mercy and leave a blessing behind him. And you transgressors, who are the cause of these tears, return, even late at last, to your heart; return, and fear the indignation of your blessed lawgiver. Consider the desolation of the order which you bring in to your own harm; fear the wrath of the Almighty, which you provoke by your crimes. Woe to us. The city of our religion is being destroyed by enemies all around us; the house of discipline is being reduced to nothing, and no one is found who resists, no one who sets himself like a wall before the house of God. We all seek the things that are our own; we all conceal the common necessity of the order, until little by little we too shall fail. Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers, our houses to outsiders. Monasteries that were consecrated as dwellings for monks are now becoming stables for clerics and strongholds of fighting soldiers. What shall I say? I am ashamed to utter what men without conscience are not ashamed to commit in the cloisters of monks: they disturb the seclusion of religious men; they change houses of prayer into dwellings of merchants. I suffer with your calamities, O venerable religion of Benedict; I groan that you are exposed to plunder by everyone who passes by. There is none to console you from among all your dear ones, because those who could help you are unwilling, and those who wish to assist you cannot.

O with what beautiful comeliness you once flourished in the Church of God, when you brought forth men distinguished by every holiness and knowledge, and, like a youth strong and steadfast, you were accustomed to drive away from yourself every dishonorable manner of life. But now, as if worn out by old age and the long oppression of days, you have failed, and the strength of your youth has been taken away, because your beauty is no longer in you. Where now is your zeal? Where is the beauty of your face? Where is your honor? Where is the power once widespread throughout the whole world? Where are your sons around your table, learned and most holy men? Where is the study of letters, venerable to God and the angels, whose ardor once made you exalted above all orders? They have already failed, and you have been reduced almost to nothing; you have lost the beauty of your youth, and the strength of your adolescence has been scattered. To what shall I compare you, or to what shall I liken you, secluded daughter? To what shall I equal you, and console you, mother of monks? Great as the sea is your contrition; who will heal you? O if you had foreseen this ruin in any way and guarded against it, how blessed all nations would call you. But you said in your abundance: I shall not be moved forever. Plenty has made you poor, and the abundance of temporal things has stripped you of all your adornment. You have begotten perverse sons, disobedient, rebellious against holy institutions, who, hiding under the honorable cloak of your [unclear], have stripped you bare of all your beauty. Alas, mother and virgin, you have grown old in a foreign land; you have been counted with the dead; there is no appearance of your beauty. Arise now, O Benedict, most holy prince of monks, and see your order, which you founded, and your inheritance, which you planted. Look upon the monks who have forgotten your profession, immersed in earthly things, given over to pleasure, all full of the springs of vices. You once gave them the best precepts for living; you commanded them to be free from the cares of secular business; you ordered their hearts to be stretched out to the love of God alone. Rise, I say, O most blessed father, and see the desolation of your order, which is confounded within by its own sons and scattered without by enemies. The monks despise the institutions of your piety; foreign men seize the monasteries of your order. There is no one to defend the honor of your name; no [unclear].

there is one who may protect the honor of your most sacred order. Rise up also, O great Pope Gregory, you who forbade, under anathema, places sacred to God belonging to monks to be transferred to secular uses; and see monks driven from monasteries, and worldly clerics thrust in. You, once the prince of all churches, used to devote the greatest care to monastic honor, taking pains with immense solicitude that nothing should be presumed in the sacred order outside the Rule of Benedict. Behold now the manner of life of monks, O most reverend prelate, stripped of all honor, full of all foulness. See how monasteries dedicated to your order are handed over into the hands of clerics, and those which once could be compared to angelic choirs now become brothels of harlots.

Rise up, most glorious emperor and unconquered defender of the Christian faith, Charles, glory of the Germans, and see the calamity of the monks: you who once made the order of Father Benedict glorious, and by your zeal spread it through almost the whole world. See now the monasteries which you once founded, all exposed to the plundering of enemies. You who once revered the monastic order as the camp of God, now have compassion, O holy prince, on it as despised by all and stripped bare of its goods. You were once accustomed, with immense care, to bring lukewarm abbots and monks back to the observance of regular discipline, and, once reformed, to defend them with immense solicitude from every harassment by your own people or by any others.

Rise up also, Berno, abbot of the monastery of Cluny, together with your successors, you who in ancient times magnificently restored the holy order when it was collapsing, and brought it back wholly to its former beauty. Rise, I say, now, and see how the iniquity of monks abounds; rage rules; crime overflows; pleasure makes almost all men go mad. The beauty of reformation has been taken away. Discipline has collapsed. Zeal for holy conduct has perished; humility has breathed its last.

Rise up, William, abbot of the monastery of Hirsau, most reverend father, you who restored the Cluniac renewal in Germany after its fall; you who provided abundant institutes for monastic conduct; you who by your prayers strengthened the limbs of the sick; you who illuminated the German nation with doctrine and holiness like a most brilliant star. Rise also, you most excellent fathers, authors of various reformations, and see that your labors have now perished: constitutions neglected, exhortations spurned, the solemn warnings of solicitude despised. By life and doctrine you made the monastic order glorious, beloved by God, venerable to angels, holy to yourselves, reverend to men.

Where now are those merits? Where now are those prayers of the saints? Alas, venerable mother Religion, to what great calamity you have come. Those who once glorified you now despise you; those who honored you now scorn you. You have abandoned the commandments of your lawgiver; you have cast aside the study of the Scriptures; therefore you have become contemptible. The sons whom you bore have done this evil to you. For as soon as monks began to savor earthly things, to neglect sacred readings, to put inward things after outward ones, your best color was changed into foulness. But what of it? He who falls often resolves to rise again; but you, once fallen, never rose again altogether.

What could Cluniac, what could Specuensian, what could [Ycalian?], what could Melk, what could the very recent Bursfelde reform, and any other reforms besides these, accomplish for the whole order, spread throughout the entire world? For although the Cluniac reform poured forth the light of its honor in all provinces of the world, nevertheless it left many monasteries in different kingdoms in their former deformity. For from that time when our religion first fell, there has never been any general reformation. O how easy is the descent to Avernus; how ready the will to sin; how very great, after a fall, is the difficulty of rising again to uprightness. All, so to speak, have fallen; few have risen from their deformity; many are rotting away in their pleasures.

I grieve over you, O flower of monastic beauty; I grieve, and indeed vehemently, and if I cannot aid you otherwise, I pour out tears both hot and most bitter for your contrition. But you also, O fathers most worthy of reverence, who love the honor of your order, who grieve over the idle crushing of our mystical Joseph, who desire to come to the inheritance [unclear], consider the state of our religion; look upon its desolation; think of a remedy. Behold, the wealthy monasteries are being snatched all around from the hands of Saint Benedict; behold

The cloisters of monks become dwellings of clerics, and from evil pursuits monks are transferred to the worst. You err, O wisdom of the world; power of the age, you are deceived: never from a bad monk will you be able to make a good canon. But you also, transgressors, take heed; apostates from the order, listen. What madness drives you, that you destroy for Saint Benedict monasteries which you did not build? Or do you think yourselves free from damnation if, after casting off the monastic garb, you sin as clerics? In the strict examination, will a presumptuous license to sin save you? Perhaps in another habit you will be unknown to [unclear]? We shall see whether God approves your transfer, when in that dread judgment, where no rank but perpetual horror dwells. For what other dwelling he is to receive, having become a worse canon from a bad monk, I do not sufficiently understand. Senseless men, and enemies to yourselves, who will teach you to flee from the wrath to come? Who will be able, or will dare, to defend your unjust cause against Saint Benedict in that dread examination? Whom will you have as advocate for your rashness? Saint Benedict, prince of monks, will stand as witness against you; he will accuse you and condemn you: who will excuse you? Do not flatter yourself, wicked contemner of the regular vow; do not soothe your conscience. If you have Benedict as your adversary, you will find none of the saints your friend. For he who offends one citizen of the heavenly fatherland [unclear]. Where there is the highest and blessed tranquility, there also will be the indivisible unity of souls. Who, then, will be able to deliver you from the hand of the Lord, if all the saints have stood against you? Call upon those who now deceive you, who take from you the habit of the order, who lead you away with flattering speeches, who stand as collaborators in your apostasy, that they may defend you from the tribulation that is at hand. For if the righteous will scarcely be saved, where will the apostate and destroyer of the holy order appear? The justice of the saint will not deliver the wicked man on that day, nor will he bring aid to himself or another. Rather, those whom you now win over to yourself with gifts and presents as such great collaborators in your presumption, then you will have as witnesses and companions of your wickedness.

There will be no defender there for a corrupt action, no advocate of iniquity, since where all things will be laid bare, there the accusing conscience will be enough for each one unto damnation. There the army of saints will stand against those who have wickedly profaned the dwellings of monks, who have impiously destroyed the order of the holy fathers. But the authors of these things, which I seem to myself justly to have called unjust, strive to excuse their deed in this way, saying: The irregularity of monks, driving monasteries to extreme poverty, cannot be corrected and amended unless it is transferred into another state, on account of the contrived reasons which they invent for themselves; these also, God granting, we shall show in what follows to be empty. They say, then: To correct bad monks by transfer is not only without sin, but is also a great part of justice and piety. But where can these things be discerned? In what manner will you teach as true the things you say? To convert bad monks to goodness is praiseworthy and holy; but to make them canons is not to amend monks, but to have corrupted them. A bad monk will never be a good canon; but a good one will not strip off the order that is his, but will cherish, honor, and love it. I do not now wish to contend in words; I do not wish to be too vehement for the hearing; I do not wish to depict the effect of this transfer, which I do not doubt will gradually come to light. If you wished to make bad monks into canons, why did you not put good men in their place? There is no change without transgression of the vow, when it is presumptuously changed for the worse. Woe to you deserters, who, so that satisfaction may be made to your pleasures, despise the order, deny the vow, and confound the rule of equity. We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, says the Apostle, so that each one may receive according as he has done in his body. What will the destroyers of monasteries receive there, who show no deference to the honor of the Almighty, who violate the covenant, who nullify the wills of saints, who despise the decrees of law? If it is good to found monasteries, it is evil, let no one doubt, to destroy them. A contrary action will receive no reward except a contrary one. Finally, if no one dares to break the last will of a dead man in legacies made to any man whatsoever, why do lovers of the world presume to usurp for themselves things offered to God and the saints

[unclear]? If one who violates a man’s testament is guilty of a crime, what punishment does he deserve who unjustly diverts to alien uses the foundations of monasteries made by holy bishops and princes? For kings, princes, and prelates, and the rest of the faithful who founded them to the honor of God and of the monastery, are proven to have wished this above all: that the foundations of this institution should obtain an inviolable effect. If they had wished to have canons in the monasteries, they would not have placed monks there. But the blind ambition of men has grown so strong that it thinks of nothing less than future things, and loves nothing more than perishable things. O every late condition of human frailty, O ever damnable forgetfulness of the commandments of God. Rights consented to sins, and what is public began to be more lawful. Offenses blaze everywhere, and here and there, through wicked minds, by manifold kinds of sin, [unclear] works harmful deceits and frauds. This man confounds the order; that man utterly destroys it. This man withdraws the will of the saints; that man writes false allegations of dismemberment. Here monks are shut out from monasteries; there the goods of the order are given to others. The enemy assails those who stand firm; the slanderer attacks; the false witness defames. Already, among the guilty, to be innocent is a crime. What love of honor could there be there, what integrity could exist in minds, where the profession of the order is deserted, where the vow made to God is revoked? What sense of shame for things remains there, what virtue could subsist, where divine right is violated, where there is no fear of the laws, no dread of the judge? What can be said more inhuman, what more cruel, than to wish to usurp divine right for oneself, to confound right and wrong, to break a vow, to withhold the worship due to God?

O that day, dreadful and horrifying to all mortals, on which, after long tolerating these evils of the monks, the wrath of God will be vindicated, on which apostates will feel the punishment owed them, because the adversaries of the holy order will pay the penalty for their rashness. What good will it then do you to have trafficked in the vow made to God, to have extinguished the sacred order, to have had a brief, shameful pleasure for a time in the flesh? When the Lord begins to count his worshippers, to give true monks the promised rewards, to separate the good from the evil, to divide the truthful from the false, what place will you receive, what success will you have, you who deny the holy profession of religion, who break vows, who despise the order, who violate faith?

Would that you considered the brevity of this life; would that you feared the examination of future recompense; would that, pierced by salutary teachings, you attended with repentance to the voice of the Lord, saying: I do not desire the death of the one who dies, but that he return and live. And through the prophet: Return to the Lord your God, because he is merciful and kind, patient and of great compassion, who may revoke the sentence, if you are willing to wash away your fault with tears. But you do not fear the judgment of God; you despise his clemency; you contemn his patience and long-suffering. Therefore the Apostle says to each of you: Do you not know that the patience of God leads you to repentance? But you, by your hardness and impenitent heart, store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the just judgment of God, who will render to each according to his works. He said that the judgment of God is just because it is late, because it is long and greatly deferred, so that God’s long patience may provide for you unto life. But how will you do penance, you who do not acknowledge your fault? You will grieve, but too late, when there will now be no place for repentance, but the repayment of vengeance. Then, therefore, punishment will repay the impious man and the sinner, when repentance for sin can no longer profit.

O what guilty men they will then remain, what wretches, what unhappy men, who, for the sake of this briefest time, did the will of the devil, so that they must be tormented with him in inextinguishable fire. Would that these things clung to the hearts of those men; would that they thought on these things, who desert their order, who break their vow, who so boldly lie both to God and to his saints. But we strive in vain; our words do not receive them, who contemn the words of God and of the Church and of Saint Benedict. Therefore this cause of the order must be carried on not with words, but with deeds. Let us therefore be armed, fathers, with all our strength, and let us prepare ourselves for the contest with incorrupt mind, devoted virtue, firm constancy, against those who desire to destroy our order, who strip off the monk, who take away monasteries, who desert the rule, who are rebellious against their visitors. Let us be armed, I beseech you, fathers, with zeal for regular discipline and with the honor of the order, sparing no labors, no expenses, lest the destructive plague, through our silence, [unclear].

successively infects the order. Never has so great a necessity lain upon our order; never has it been enveloped in so many evils. See, monks cast off the habit; monasteries are turned into dwellings of clerics; and while we attend to private advantages, while we flee labors, while we spare expenses, while we serve our own avarice, the order perishes, religion passes away, the worship of God vanishes. Many monasteries have already, through the wickedness of the times, not to say our own sloth, been transferred away from the order; and unless we keep watch otherwise, the rashness of wicked men threatens that greater losses must be inflicted upon us. Certainly, where the audacity of fools is not at once repressed, an occasion for attempting similar things is offered to the rest. What shall I say of the monks whom we still have in the order by habit and tonsure alone? And, lest we put the members before the head, what is more wretched in this unhappy time than deformed abbots? They care for nothing less than the Rule; they pursue nothing more zealously than lust, avarice, pleasure, pride, and the vanity of the world. Thus, when the head is infected, all the members of the body are corrupted. Now in monasteries where the Rule is despised, where discipline is not observed, what else is seen than a certain spring of all vices? No obedience, no poverty, no chastity is held among them out of love of virtue; among them, to live without crime is a crime. These are corrupt men, perverse monks, craftsmen of deceit, authors of fraud, ministers of iniquity, friends of wickedness; they flee discipline, now despise observance, destroy the order, confound unity. And truly, fathers, unless you quickly provide remedies for these evils, in a short time you will see the order diminished, and you will grieve for it. But perhaps you say: vigilance has never been lacking; our diligence has never ceased; we have always opposed the rashness of evil men; we have always tried to prevent the dismemberment of monasteries, and we have never accomplished anything. What do our labor, our efforts, our heavy expenses accomplish, when princes and rectors of churches oppose themselves so powerfully? I know, fathers, that what you say is true; I know the deeds, I know they have been continued. But I beg you not to take my words in a bad sense, if I dare to answer these objections. Your vigilance in the causes of the order is known to me; your labors are evident; the magnitude of the expenses is proven; perseverance in these matters has always been applied.

But I should like you to remember, O fathers, two verses of Horace in which he says: There is measure in things, and finally there are fixed limits, beyond and short of which what is right cannot stand. We have many and different adversaries; one must not fight against all in one manner, but in different ways, in varied ways, with discretion. We are monks, professors of humility; the battle must be begun by us with prayers, entreaties, and supplications; high Jupiter must not be provoked by ferocity; a headlong sentence must not be brought against the gods. Divine powers are placated by prayers, not by threats. But enough of this. For I believe, fathers, that you understand what I mean. Nor are these things to be explained indiscriminately to everyone, but only to those who have zeal for the order and the power to carry it out.
Against those who transfer themselves from the order, or have already long since transferred themselves. Chapter 3.

Whether I am justly moved enough against those who try to dismember themselves from our order, I do not sufficiently know; and if I did know, I would hardly dare to say, since the patience of the Almighty tolerates them so long and lashes them so late. But when I look upon the end of those who have already long since dismembered themselves from the order, I consider this long-suffering of God’s patience sufficiently avenged by strict chastisement. For, as we have learned from the report of those who knew many of them, few of those who cast off the monk died a good death. Rather, called suddenly from this life without signs of penitence and without the ecclesiastical sacraments, they gave a manifest indication of their own unhappiness. What, then, shall we say to these things? Shall we rejoice in the destruction of the dying? Far be it. It is the Lord who long tolerates sinners here so that they may be converted; it is he who condemns more harshly those who are not converted. But we, with the prophet, fear his sentence, saying: You are just, O Lord, and your judgment is right. But the just man, by whatever death he has been overtaken, will be in refreshment. Concerning the impious, however, the prophet says: The death of sinners is most evil. We, however, bring back to mind the ruin of the wicked for this reason: that at least by fear the rest—

[unclear] back from the evil undertaking. But how will they receive our words, who mock those above and those below? Unless deeds are added to words, exhortations accomplish nothing among malicious minds. Still the stiff-necked people murmurs in the desert; still the impious nation blasphemes its lawgiver; still the wicked nation resolves to return into Egypt. They fear lest they die in the wilderness, when they ought to have feared this alone: lest they die outside the wilderness.

O hard mind of men, O ruinous freedom of monks, how long does your cruelty rage, which does not know how to spare even those whom it has as authors and friends? He who is worthless to himself, to whom will he be good? O unheard-of zeal of monks, O monstrous crime: to mock God, to deny him what was promised, to break faith, to withdraw the service owed. What is more cruel than this impiety, what more wicked than this sacrilege? O perverse monk, O unjust apostate, O most wicked perjurer, how long do you set yourself against the kindness of God, how long do you mock the mercy of the Almighty? You are a monk; as a monk too you will be judged, even if you have put off the skin together with the habit. Why do you depart from the holy order? Why do you lie to God? Believe me: the Almighty will not give his honor to another; he will not forgive you forever what he once solemnly accepted as an offering. Before you made your promise to God you were free and of your own choice; but after you promised, you began to belong to God. Now it is not lawful for you to abandon what belongs by right to God. Your voice has bound you to God: either you will be saved as a monk, or otherwise you will not be saved.

Behold, before your eyes is the way of life and the way of death; choose whichever you wish. If you keep faith with God, if you fulfill your promise, you will have reward; if you deny it, you will receive punishment for contempt. Hence Paul, admonishing you, says: Brothers, do not err; God is not mocked. For whatever a man has sown, that also will he reap. What do you presume you will receive, you who sow in the flesh? For he says: Those who sow in the flesh, from the flesh also will reap. But the fruit of the flesh has no share in the inheritance of the saints. Why then do you deceive yourself? Why do you trust vainly in vanity? Why do you transgress the ancient bounds which the holy fathers set? The vow which you solemnly made to God you deny, and yet you expect a portion with the elect of God as though righteous.

There is no peace for the impious with the sons of God. Behold, you squander the inheritance of the Lord; you enrich strangers from the goods of the holy father Benedict; you deny your promise; and, so that you may sin freely, you heap up false things as true. If you are a good monk, do not desert your purpose; do not abandon the seclusion of the monastery. But if you are a bad monk, you will never be a good canon. For he who is not good is bad; and he who is bad is not as he ought to be, and therefore is unjust. But the unjust have no share in the kingdom of God. And it matters little where you are, so long as, being bad everywhere and wretched everywhere, you are tormented. Unless perhaps you wish to be liable to a double damnation, so that, while you are a bad monk and an unjust canon, guilty and false in both places, you demand the wages of both.

Nor should you object to me the dispensation of the Roman pontiff, which, unless God approves it, will by no means excuse you. Not all things please God which are done on earth by the supreme pontiff. Now if you cry out and are angry with me, as though I were judging the acts of the vicar of Christ, I answer: I embrace, honor, and venerate the supreme pontiff as the true vicar of Christ; I by no means reprehend his deeds, but I know that he is a man, and that as a man he can both be deceived and deceive. No wonder. For in so great a care of all the churches, in so great an occupation with affairs, when false things are reported as true, a mind distracted in many matters is easily deceived.

But you, apostate from a holy order, who think yourself secure because of a bull of dispensation, see to it that after death, as the common saying goes, you do not meet an illiterate demon, one who does not know letters, who does not defer to an appeal, who despises the bindings of your immunity. Believe me: there is no craft that can deceive God. O wretchedly unhappy man, O senseless apostate, what will you answer to Saint Benedict concerning the profession which you spurn? What will you answer to the almighty ones concerning the vow which you contemn? Whom will you be able to appoint as advocate of your case in that dreadful judgment, where nothing can lie hidden? There all things will be naked, all things open; there no place of saving repentance is now left; there the space for making excuse is denied to all. What will that dispensation rashly presumed here profit you there, when it will be permitted neither to prove it by testimony nor to defend it by law? Then you will see, O perverse monk; then you will understand what strength it contained in itself

may a licence fraudulently obtained [unclear], when you have felt the vengeance of the eternal Judge in punishment. Why do you plead dispensation to me? Why do you proclaim a licence to sin? Do you think that by the authority of the supreme pontiff you can escape the wrath of God? I dare to say: the pope’s dispensation will profit you nothing if it has been obtained by fraud, by deceit, by falsehood, or unjustly. That is not good, that is not just, which is acquired by evil arts. For a dispensation to be just, four things are required, without which a dispensation will by no means save you. What are they? Necessity, namely, congruity, usefulness, and honorableness. But you, perjured monk, who are led by mere willfulness, who despise God and your order, invent necessity, show a false congruity, lie about usefulness, and fashion honorableness by fraud. Let necessity be evident and manifest, congruity true, usefulness not private but public, honorableness not fictitious but proper; otherwise the dispensation will be unjust.

Indeed, I have nothing for which I should be angry with the supreme pontiff in this dispensation; I reprehend nothing in his actions, since I am not unaware that he was circumvented by the false narratives of monks. You are the guilty ones, you deceitful men, you who must be marked for wickedness, O perverse monks, criminal apostates, who by lying, deceit, and fraud seek what you despair of obtaining by just prayers. What necessity urges you to desert your order and pass over into the state of secular life? What congruity recommends breaking what, once promised to God, no one may revoke? What usefulness is there in laying aside the monastic habit, deserting the order, denying your purpose, transferring the monastery, and not only breaking but utterly casting away the vow made to God in the presence of all the saints? Or what honorableness is it for a monk dedicated to God to return to the world, break faith, commit perjury, and perpetrate sacrilege? Workers of evil and impious men, how will you ever be able to excuse such a wicked presumption? None of these four agrees with your transfer; none of them confirms your dispensation. For what necessity could have driven you to this rashness? What cause for this dismemberment could you have alleged before the vicar of Christ? The poverty and ruin of the monasteries. But you could have quickly restored this if you lived according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.
For a dispensation to be just, four [things are required], etc.

For you have been made poor by wicked morals; by holy conduct you would again be enriched. Look around you at monasteries restored to regular observance: how, after extreme poverty, with the Lord bestowing it, they now advance again to their former riches. And this, indeed, quite justly. For the Lord promised us in the Gospel, saying: First seek the kingdom of God and his justice, and all these things shall be added unto you. But you put aside the love of God, neglect his worship, devote yourselves to games, banquets, drunkenness, and gluttony, and do not regard the work of the Lord. You care nothing for regular observance; therefore, because spiritual things have been neglected, by the just judgment of God temporal things too have failed you. False, then, is the necessity that you invent, and insufficient the dispensation that you allege. But perhaps you say: We are not sons of rustic men but of nobles, noble, delicate, and weak. We cannot keep the observance of servants, farmers, and shepherds; fasts, abstinence, vigils, disciplines, and the other exercises they have are unbearable for us, which we neither can nor ought to imitate. What then? Are you not a monk because you are noble, because delicate, because weak? There is nothing by which you can defend yourself against Saint Benedict, who in the Rule provided abundantly for every estate, every rank, every age; who with the greatest discretion came to the aid of the delicate and the weak. Are you the only ones from among the noble, tender, and delicate who have professed the monastic order? Many most noble young men, sons of emperors, kings, dukes, and princes, have shone in our order in holiness and learning under regular observance at various times; they, nobler, more delicate, and more tender than you, yet preserving cenobitic discipline inviolate, will stand against you in testimony, easily able to prove to those who love God that what you, full of [unclear], cast away as if unbearable [unclear]. Nor do I bid you imitate the observance which you despise as that of cobblers, but the Rule which you promised, which you vowed, which you pledged yourself before God to keep. If anything in our conduct displeases you, you have the Rule; go to its precepts, shape your life. No one exacts more from you; no one requires more. The exercises of monks which you condemn in observers of the Rule, the Rule itself teaches, the Rule itself commands; and if you refuse to imitate them, by the very sentence of your own mouth

[You promised?] conversion of morals; for the Rule of Saint Benedict enjoins upon those professed under it fasts, abstinence, vigils, disciplines, obedience, patience, humility, poverty, and the other exercises of monastic discipline. These things, which you judge hard and burdensome, are so proper to the Rule that without them no one deserves to be called a monk.

Tell me, I ask, transgressor of your vow and of your order, tell me: do you still wish to live blessedly? Do you still hope that you can come to eternal life? You will answer: “That question you ask is foolish. Who would not wish to live blessedly? Who does not hope to come to eternal life? Therefore I both desire to live blessedly and trust that I can come to the heavenly fatherland.” If, then, it is so, if you trust that you will receive the blessed life, why do you abandon, spurn, and despise the way that leads to it?

You are mistaken, wretched unhappy man; you are deceived. One does not come to the kingdom except through humility, nor to rest except through labor, through abstinence, through obedience, through poverty. For Scripture says: “Through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God.” But you, unhappy apostate, who cast away the order, spurn humility, refuse obedience, hate poverty, despise patience: by what rashness do you presume to such heights? If the mouth that lies kills the soul, unless you do penance you have no share in the kingdom of Christ and of God, you who lie not to man but to God, who violate the pact, who deny the faith, who retract the vow of religion made to God.

The dispensation of the Roman pontiff, which you seek by fraud, recount with falsehood, and extort by importunate petitions, will not save you, I dare to say. For the four things which we said make a dispensation due we see to have come together not at all in your frauds. For that transfer which you make from a holy order is neither useful nor necessary, and for that reason is unfitting and dishonorable. In it, indeed, will is put in place of necessity, pleasure in place of utility, carnality in place of fittingness, impiety in place of honorableness. Is this the due occasion for your dispensation?

Keep for yourself your little letters obtained by fraud; keep the instruments of denial and apostasy. It is good for me to rest under the Rule of the most pious father Benedict, in which, if I have offended in anything through frailty, I trust that I have him as a pious advocate before the strict Judge; whose order I love, venerate, and guard with such diligence as I can. But I do not know what patron you will have, you who cast away the order, offend all the saints, and publicly lie to God. For the Rule shows that he who, after profession of the order, lives otherwise than he promised is to be condemned as a mocker of almighty God. For it has this: “Therefore, if he has acted otherwise, let him know that he is to be condemned by him whom he mocks.”

Hear these things, sons of Belial; deserters of the order, attend, and if there is any sense in you, tremble. “Let him know,” it says, “that the converted monk is to be condemned by him whom he mocks.” What greater mockery, what crime more wicked than to deny the faith promised to God, to set aside the vow, to lie to him, to withdraw service from him? I wonder, and indeed greatly, whether ever, even for an hour, apostates so criminal can have true joy, because of the confusion of conscience and the remorse of synderesis. But, to confess plainly what I think, I can be induced by no persuasions to believe that they will thereafter ever live without the very grave torment of their conscience.

By probable experience we have learned that the monks of whom we speak, after the transfer of order, become almost mad: prone to every shameful work, desperate, without devotion, without affection, without piety, without conscience, without honorableness, [unclear], troubled, witless, and obstinate; so much so that they care nothing, notice nothing, wish to hear nothing about God, about his kingdom, about purgatory, about hell, about death, about virtue, about seemly conduct. And in them is fulfilled that saying of the wise man: “When the impious man has come into the depth of evils, he despises.” And he always presumes that with a troubled and defiled conscience. Hence such apostates, as if freed from long imprisonment, boldly hurl themselves into every vice, and compensate for the shortness of time by the magnitude of their crimes.

They are offended if anyone wishes to speak before them about the love of God, the study of the Scriptures, or the honorableness of life. Nor is it any wonder if they cannot hear the words of God, to whom after so unspeakable an apostasy they prove unfaithful. They have hated the one who rebukes in the gate; they do not admit the words of salvation; they despise the sermon of penance. Therefore the wise man says: “Consider the works of God, because no one can correct him whom he has despised.” If God ever despises some men

[unclear] could not: they are surely among the first who, after their vow, prove unfaithful to him. Hence, being so despised, they rarely have recourse to repentance. Therefore let them know that they are to be condemned by him whom they mock. For they are guilty of a double sacrilege, because they unjustly take themselves away from God and monasteries away from Saint Benedict. And whoever supplied occasion, favor, counsel, and aid to these [dismemberments?] has done this irrecoverable harm to the order and to Saint Benedict. For the rule of law says: He who gives occasion for damage is deemed to have caused the damage. Therefore such men are liable to the holy lawgiver of monks and bound to restitution. Let them see how they will answer at the last judgment to God and his saints, whose temporal goods they unjustly usurp for themselves or for others.

Woe to those who unjustly take what belongs to others, which they can never restore either in this life or in the future. Woe also to you, apostate and renegade monks, who confound right, despise equity, and violate faith and covenant. Woe also to you abbots, who do not correct the evil pursuits of your monks, who consent to their apostasy, and who yourselves apostatize from the order with them. O abbot, shepherd and idol, who make wolves from sheep and secular men from monks, what answer will you have to give to the supreme shepherd when you are compelled to render account of your stewardship? What will you say to Saint Benedict when he demands back his sheep from you? He will require monks from you, not canons. What then will you answer him? Are canons monks?

When that day comes, to be feared by all mortals, on which the just judge will render to each according to his works, Benedict, the lawgiver of monks, doubt not, will accuse you gravely. Against you he will bring forth as witnesses all the true monks of his order, who will cry out unanimously to the judge: Just judge, Jesus Christ, who know all things, behold the madness, crime, sacrilege, and cruelty of this apostate, who destroyed the holy order, called monks back to the world, broke faith, and with unheard-of presumption violated the vow made to you and to us. Wretched man, what will you do, accused so gravely? Where will you flee from the face of the fury of the Lord? To whom will you have recourse? There will be no place to flee, but you will stand before the tribunal of Christ to receive a harsh sentence, unless here, through repentance and tears, you have taken care to come before the face of the Lord.

No place will be granted for excuse when you have been accused in the judgment of him who knows all things. For whatever you may wish to say will be nothing, because, accused outwardly and inwardly by the testimony of conscience, you will be judged worthy of condemnation. You seize the things that belong to divine right, you who had been appointed their guardian; therefore you will hear the Lord saying: Pay what you owe. That is: give back the monks whom I entrusted to your faith; give back the monastery which you received to govern; give back faith; give back the vow; give back holiness; give back gain; give back merit; give back honor. Pay what you owe.

I appointed you shepherd of my sheep, so that you might preserve them in holy religion, teach them, instruct them, amend them, and correct those who sinned. But you hated discipline and cast [my?] words behind you; if you saw a thief, you ran with him, and with adulterers you placed your portion. Intent on the pleasures of the flesh, you did not guard my sheep; therefore pay what you owe. After monks came from the world to religious life, they became subject to my right, and it is not lawful for them to return any further to the world. But you were appointed minister of my sheep, not lord, nor was it lawful for you in any way to alienate, usurp, or plunder anything belonging to my right. You were guardian of my things, not owner; you ought faithfully to preserve what had been acquired and to seek what had been scattered.

But you, forgetful of me, squandered my inheritance, scattered the sheep, indeed made beasts from sheep, enemies from servants, and faithless men from allies. Now therefore pay what you owe. I entrusted monks to you, whom you ought to have preserved in their holy purpose: to raise up the fallen, care for the sick, restore the failing, kindle the sluggish with charity, rouse the negligent, rebuke sinners, correct the disobedient, restrain the dissolute, and hold back the perverse from their evil pursuits. But you took care of none of those things which [unclear] by office; given over to greed, lust, and gluttony, you not only permitted monks to return to the world, but, utterly forgetful of pastoral care, you also became the leader and companion of their apostasy. Now therefore give back what [was entrusted?] to your faith, not to say to your treachery. But because you will not be able to give it back, you will be cast into a dark prison covered with the gloom of death; from there you will not come out until you pay the debt, which you will never pay. There

[not only?] will you receive punishment for your own deeds, but also for all the sins of those committed to your governance whom you have neglected to correct. For thus Saint Benedict says in the Rule: Let the abbot know that the fault of the shepherd falls upon him, if the father of the household has been able to find any lack of profit in his sheep. Therefore, abbot, whoever you are, if you are wise, if you understand, if indeed you believe in the judgment to come, if you desire to escape the torments of hell, do not yield to the depraved desires of monks; do not consent to criminal dismemberments. What does pleasure profit you in this most brief life, for which you are compelled to receive eternal punishments? Do not, I beg you, do not inflict so great an injury upon Saint Benedict; do not take from him the monasteries which neither you nor all your forefathers built. Let it be enough for you that you are abbot, because you live from his patrimony. Do not forsake the order; do not consent to devilish suggestions; do not make your monks secular; do not resign the monastery entrusted to you into the hands of others. Know yourself to be a man subject to death, of brief life upon the earth. Do not do so ruinous a thing; do not commit this crime; do not perpetrate so immeasurable a sacrilege. Remain in the holy order, and do not forsake your profession, if you desire to come to eternal life. For the Lord says: He who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is not fit for the kingdom of God. Behold, you have put your hand to the ploughshare; behold, with Lot you have gone out of Sodom. If you look back, if you corrupt your profession, if you return to the world, you are not fit for the kingdom of God, and you will by no means deserve to receive it. But if you persevere in your renewal, if you keep your good will, if you have the charity of God in your heart, believe me: even if in some respects you have lived negligently, you will find Saint [Benedict?] a kindly intercessor with God, for love of whom you did not wish to forsake the order when you could have done so. Remember, I beseech you, the covenant of the Lord which you made with him when you entered the order; and do not be unfaithful to your Redeemer; do not break your vow; do not violate the pact with so wicked a perjury. Consider the pact; attend to the condition; and take care that you not prove a liar to God. Before you promised him, you were free; but after you promised, you were no longer free, but were made a servant of God. It is not lawful for you thereafter to abandon this servitude voluntarily assumed; nor is it lawful for you anywhere after profession to return to the world. But if you corrupt your profession, if you deny your vow, if you return to the world, God will not have you in that rank in which he would previously have had you, before you entered the monastery. For before your entrance into religion you were, as it were, of the household of the Lord, among his subjects and laborers. You were, I say, a creature of God; you were a servant; you were a slave; but you were not a friend, an officer, an intimate, a secretary. But after you became a monk, you promised fidelity to the Lord, that you would cleave to him continually, that where the Lord is, there you too would be, his minister. He chose you as a friend and, so to speak, as guardian of his body, that in his sight you should always minister to him and fulfill his will in all things. For this you promised. Therefore, if you withdraw from him to whom you vowed yourself, if you are found unfaithful and a despiser of your vow, he will not have you of his household as before, before you became a monk, but certainly as a fugitive, unfaithful, a transgressor, perjured, and lying. For the monk who denies his vow denies Christ. For blessed Jerome says: I, who seem to be a monk, if I corrupt my profession, have denied Christ. But you transgressors, who, despising the sacred order, have from monks been made canons: you, I say, have not only corrupted your profession, but, what is more wicked, have utterly destroyed it. Now therefore either you have denied Christ, or what Jerome says is false. But because what so great a man taught cannot be false, it remains that you are deniers of Christ, perjured and unfaithful. Would that at least, though late, you would at last undergo the remedies of penitence, you who are placed in such great dangers. If he has denied Christ who violates the monastic profession, what does he deserve who defrauds the whole order, and finally all the saints, of what is due? If he always burns who unjustly occupies the professions [unclear] of men, of what punishment is he worthy who usurps goods dedicated to God and the saints for himself? If, according to ecclesiastical tradition, he sins mortally who unjustly claims for his own use another's house or field, of how great a crime is he guilty who [unclear] the house and possessions of God and of the saints [unclear] of things unduly taken away, man is bound to man; how much more are those who take monasteries from God and Saint Benedict bound to restitution. If pec

sin is not forgiven unless he restores what has been taken away. When will those be able to be absolved from guilt who turn the dwellings of the servants of God to alien uses, and monasteries, once taken away, will never be brought back to the order? Woe to those who did not fear to draw up for themselves this testament, which they will be able to revoke by no satisfaction whatever. O monk, O abbot, you who revoke your vow solemnly made to God, who cast off the habit of holy religion, who transfer monasteries consecrated to Saint Benedict into the hands of clerics: what will you answer when accused before almighty God? Perhaps you will say: We have changed the vow for the better, since indeed they are not ignorant of the difference of a vow. To live as a canon is good and holy, if a man has been called by God to that state. But if he has been called to the rank of monastic perfection, it will never be lawful for him to descend to the canonicate. For no one doubts that canons are inferior to monks.

Tell me, whoever you are, who are a cooperator in the depravity of monks, who transfer them from the order, who defend unjust causes against God and Saint Benedict, who are held to be the favorer and patron of their apostasy. Tell me, then, what seems to you? Is it lawful for monks professed in a holy order to take off the habit and become secular canons? If it is lawful, why do you obtain, with such expense, labors, wearisome efforts, and importunate princes, the dispensation of the Roman pontiff? For lawful things do not need dispensation. But if it is unlawful, who will make it lawful? A dispensation? I very much doubt it. Whether the pope can dispense in this matter or cannot is not mine to discuss, since it is agreed that he has the fullness of power. Far be it from me, therefore, to derogate even in the least from the authority of the supreme pontiff. For he is the vicar of Christ, and it is not lawful for a man to judge anything concerning him. Therefore are you secure if he does what he seems able to do? Believe me, you are not secure, because you have told a false cause for your transfer; you have fraudulently deceived the vicar of Christ, because both the narrative was false and the supplication, not to say extortion, was importunate.

Finally, the bull of your transfer, written carefully and cautiously, does not absolve you from the order, nor remove the vow, nor take away religion, nor consent to laying aside the monastic habit. Do you think that the supreme pontiff wishes to entangle his conscience in your sins? Read the bull attentively; consider the words; note the intention of the one dispensing; and you will find that even after the dispensation you are a monk before God and the Church. For I have both seen and read the bull of this transfer, in which the pope consents that monks may have prebends and benefices, and nevertheless commands that they render to Saint Benedict what they have vowed. He grants them the habit of the canonicate, but by no means takes away the monastic garb. See how secure you are, who transgress the limits of the indult, who fashion false things as true, who lie to the vicar of Christ, who extort bulls no less than you obtain them.

In those matters that are of positive law, a dispensation makes lawful what otherwise was not lawful, if a reasonable cause requires it. But you are commanded by divine law to render the vow made to God, from which the pope never intends to absolve you without necessity. But tell me, I ask you: what is the cause of your transfer? You will perhaps answer what all those so transferred are accustomed to answer: There are many causes, which necessarily drove us to this matter. What, then, are they? The poverty of the monastery, the incursions of enemies, the exaction of princes, the bad rule of abbots. These are the causes of our transfer. But a web of spiders, fashioned with blood, is easily broken, if anything of weight is placed upon it. You apostates, however, narrate false things as true, and under the fiction of poverty deceive the vicar of Christ, indeed your very selves. Would that your poverty were what you allege; would that you had less earthly substance, as you falsely pretend. Why do you allege poverty, you who possess the greatest riches? Who does not know that the monastery of Saint Alban, before it could be transferred in temporal matters, always abounded in many riches? What shall I say of Ellwangen, once a distinguished monastery, whose riches could have sufficed for a prince? Surely the monastery of Saint Burkhard ought not to have been transferred on account of poverty, since to this very day it exceeds all the monasteries of that province in riches. What shall I say of Seltz, what of Klingenmuenster, monasteries most abundant as far as moderate measure is concerned? Surely in their transfer poverty could not truthfully have been alleged?

O betrayers of your order and transgressors of your vow, do you believe that lying words can remain hidden? Your deceits are not concealed from us, nor are we ignorant of the riches which you deny. If you were poor, as you pretend, you could not expend for your transfer some two thousand, others four thousand florins, and some even more. Why then do you allege poverty, you who are not poor? Why do you say that you have nothing from which you can live as monks, you who can expend such great sums of money so as to become canons? Finally, if the poverty of the monasteries oppresses you, why do you not undertake reform? Why do you not bring private possessions, contrary to the rule, back to common use? For while each man loves his own purse, the state of the community falls. If, according to the rule which you have professed, you lived without property of your own, by the Lord’s providence you would abound in all riches. But you, neglecting spiritual things, devote your labor to the pleasure of the flesh; for this reason you have come down to lack of temporal goods. I would have said these things against those who, because of contempt for spiritual goods, also suffer want of temporal goods. But those who transferred themselves from the order, if they had been poor, would have persevered in it. For there is need of many expenses, costs, and provisions, which the poor could never have laid out. Therefore those who take poverty as the cause of their transfer are lying. As for the fact that they allege wars, battles, and the devastations of enemies as a defense of their dismemberment, there is no prudent person who does not know that this is frivolous, vain, and insufficient. For all the things they recount can be hostile no less to canons than to monks. But when they call the rule of the abbot among the causes, it is not undeservedly ascribed to the fault of those whose election sets a bad ruler over the monastery. And not undeservedly. As the monks are, so is the abbot of the monks. For bad monks are judged unworthy of a good abbot. Finally, if the abbot is bad, how does a good provost arise? You ought to have sought other remedies from experienced men, by which you might make progress in the order without complaint. But he seeks an occasion who wishes to withdraw from a friend; he invents countless causes who desires to dismember himself from the order. Now he has exhausted the debts of the monastery, now he falsely asserts the hardship of hostility, now he invents a harsh lordship, now he blames the sloth of prelates. He seeks everything, he takes up everything, so that he may either disparage the whole order or show the place unfit for regular observance. “If,” he says, “most blessed father, such a monastery is transferred into a secular church, especially the divine worship is thereby increased; it will make princes beholden to the Roman Church; it will prepare peace round about for the peoples, and the greatest honor for the Christian name.” O deceitful tongue, O lying lip, O contriver of deceit, O inventor of fraud, O minister of iniquity, who recount false things for true, evil things for good, sacrilegious things for holy. Kings and princes have been accustomed to build monasteries, not also to destroy them; you ought not mendaciously to have alleged them as patrons of your treachery. For if they seek the praise of God, they will never consent that monasteries be transferred from the holy order. But if they wish to consider their own advantages, they are accustomed to receive more profit from monasteries than from collegiate churches. Whence, then, comes such unheard-of presumption to you, that before the vicar of Christ you should falsely claim as pleasing to princes a matter which is known to be contrary to them? Thus you act, thus you deceive the vicar of Christ, master of evil, deviser of deceit, inventor of lying, author of crime, craftsman of iniquity, you who live by fraud, who fortify yourself with impiety, who attack religion, who gape after gains, who are fed by pleasure, to whom everything consists in crime and nothing in the love of God. Far be it from faithful princes that they should take away from Saint Benedict the monasteries which their once devout forebears built for him. Woe to you, perverse monk, who presume to inflict such great insult on the order, that you destroy monasteries which neither you nor your parents built. Woe also to you who give patronage to evil matters against God and his saints, who entangle yourself in the sins of others, who sell your tongue, who for a paltry price incur the indignation of God and of all the saints. Woe to you, I say, advocate of reprobate monks, who do injury to God, who by wicked work mock his saints, who deny the right of equity, who by words and deeds exhort monks to return to the world. O what will you answer almighty God when [unclear] of all your

an account of works will be required. When you are accused by Saint Benedict as the destroyer, as it were, of his order, what then will you set against the accusation of the saints? What will you answer? How will you excuse yourself? Who is going to make a distinct plea to the judge for your deliverance? What advocate will you then be able to have, you who now are the advocate of the wicked against God? Would that you were wise and understood; would that you looked to the end, and by no means entangled yourself in the sins of others. But, inflamed by the torches of avarice, you think only of the gains of this life; you show that you have no understanding at all of future calamities. Therefore, just as birds are caught in a snare, so in your sins and in those of the men whom you made apostatize from the order, when you do not expect it, you will be caught. O how harsh a sentence they will receive by whose counsel monks have despised their order. You lied about a great advantage in the petition, you who intend only this: that you may disgracefully empty out the honor of the order. Is this how the worship of God is increased? Is this that peace promised round about to men? You will never make bad monks into good canons. But he who makes men bad, what does he deserve except the reward of the bad? Monks who, having despised the order, return to the world are bad. For unless they were bad and sinners, they would by no means have deserted the holy order. For no one hates the good except a bad man; no one withdraws from the holy purpose that he vowed except a perverse man. But he who offers himself as patron to perverse men in evil causes makes himself a participant in the sins of others. To be a good canon in the church of God is holy; but to be a monk for the love of God is of greater perfection. A canon is permitted to pass over to monks as to a higher grade, but a monk is forbidden to descend to canons. Nor will a dispensation make lawful what has been obtained by false accounts. If there is necessity in the petition, integrity in the intention of the petitioner, and honorableness in the use of the dispensation, I say boldly that the pope can dispense with a monk so that he may become a canon, yet in such a way that he is not absolved without necessity from that by which he is known to be bound to God. For I am certain that the supreme pontiff intends to absolve no one from any approved religious order without evident common advantage and manifest necessity. But the advocates of apostates recount false causes as true ones; they fabricate necessity; they lie about advantage; they pretend to honorableness, which they flee. The root and cause of this whole evil is founded on pleasure alone and hatred of discipline. But when the cause of the account is false, the dispensation does not free the one who obtained it, but condemns him. The supreme pontiff, after hearing the accounts of petitioners, is accustomed to answer cautiously: “If it is so,” he says, “as is related, let what is requested be done, in the manner and form that follows.” He answers cautiously; he grants secretly; and, once the dispensations have been heard under fixed limits, they are transgressed, while they consider not what they have obtained but what they wished to obtain. O senseless misery, O unhappy men, why do you deceive yourselves? Why do you voluntarily destroy your souls? The intention of the dispenser does not absolve you from what you promised to Saint Benedict. But you usurp more for yourselves than the pope granted; indeed you assume the whole without permission, which you unlawfully desired to obtain. It is true what a certain man, still surviving among us, said about some of us, when, with excommunication, he had stripped them of the monastic habit: “And if,” he says, “I have taken off the habit from them, nevertheless, according to the tenor of the bull, they are still monks before God.” Unhappy apostates, who will deliver you from the hand of the living God? Who will be able to defend you from the accusation of Saint Benedict? What will it profit you that here you have been made canons from ex-monks without attack, if at the last judgment of God it happens that you are numbered with the reprobate? For truly, unless Saint Benedict, prince of monks, consents, no dispensation excuses you. Your transfer does not have regard to the proper end, and for that reason it will be inexcusable. Question your consciences, and consider with what intention you withdrew from the order. If for the love of God, if from desire for the heavenly homeland, if for the salvation of souls, if for the advancement of virtues and the state of a holier life, you had put off the habit. But in all these things your intention was contrary; therefore the transfer from the order is deservedly judged alien to the will of God. For, in order that you might live without law, you cast off the habit, without obedience, without humility, without

to live in poverty. This was your first intention. The fear of God is not before your eyes. You think nothing of the salvation of souls. You have no understanding of eternal life. You desire to walk in the pleasure of the flesh alone. All the causes and reasons that you related in your petition are fabricated and false. How will the dispensation be lawful? How will the authority of the supreme pontiff excuse you, which you did not fear to circumvent by falsehood, fraud, deceit, and importunate prayers? What should be thought of you, your conduct, once examined, has declared. For the Lord says in the Gospel about ravening wolves: By their fruits you shall know them. Never is true joy seen among you because of it; never can the conscience be secure, but it is always anxious over its guilt, always troubled, since they have the devil as an inciter to despair, by whose prompting you have withdrawn from the order of necessity. Hence it is that you are not at all solicitous about the love of God and the salvation of souls, but, intent on earthly vanities and carnal desires, you think of nothing less than eternal life. By what spirit this transfer was made among you, your way of life shows. For those who are led by the spirit of God have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires. But you are not so. For as soon as you cast off the habit of religion, like wanton oxen, released from the yoke of subjection, you plunge yourselves, as if lawfully, into every disgrace; you cast off all honor; you make a pact with vices and wage war against virtues. The charity of God is not in your hearts. You despise mercy and piety. You love vanity, and you have become vain. You are evil to all good men, worse to monks, worst to yourselves. A transfer that has opened an entrance to vices has not been made for the better. Deserters of the love of God and of the order, enemies of honor, adversaries of piety: if you love God, if you are good, if you love religion, why do you hate monks? But you hate especially those who have persevered in the order from which you have fallen away, because, when you see those men now standing firmly in their vocation, you fear their testimony against you in judgment.
